questions.stem: A particle moves in a straight line. At time \(t\) seconds, its displacement is \(x\) metres from the origin \(O\). Its velocity is given by \(v = 2-4\cos 2t\), for \(0 \le t \le 2\pi\).

parts.stem: (a) Find the initial velocity of the particle.

steps.explain: Substitute \(t=0\) into the velocity function.
Evaluate.

parts.stem: (b) Find all the times when the particle is at rest, where \(0 \le t \le 2\pi\).
parts.hint: At rest means \(v=0\). Solve \(2-4\cos 2t = 0\), being careful with the doubled domain for the angle \(2t\).

steps.explain: Set the velocity to zero and isolate \(\cos 2t\).
Since \(0\le t\le 2\pi\), the angle \(2t\) ranges over \(0 \le 2t \le 4\pi\) — two full revolutions. List all solutions for \(2t\) where cosine equals \(\tfrac12\) in that extended range.
Divide every solution by 2 to get \(t\).

parts.stem: (c) Sketch the graph of \(v\) as a function of \(t\), showing all key features.

steps.explain: Mark the key features already found: initial value \(v=-2\) at \(t=0\), and the four rest times (\(v=0\)) from part (b).
The function oscillates between a minimum of \(v=2-4=-2\) and a maximum of \(v=2+4=6\), completing one full cosine cycle every \(\pi\) seconds (since the angle is \(2t\)).
Sketch the full curve over \(0\le t\le 2\pi\), matching the graph shown above.
steps.work: Curve as shown, with maxima at \(t=\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{3\pi}{2}\) (\(v=6\)) and minima at \(t=0, \pi, 2\pi\) (\(v=-2\)).

parts.stem: (d) Find the acceleration of the particle when \(t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\).
parts.hint: Acceleration is \(\ddot{x} = \dfrac{dv}{dt}\). Differentiate \(v\), then substitute \(t=\pi/2\) — or note that \(t=\pi/2\) is a turning point of \(v\) on the graph in part (c).

steps.explain: Differentiate the velocity function to get acceleration.
Substitute \(t=\pi/2\).
Evaluate — this matches the graph in part (c), where \(t=\pi/2\) is a maximum turning point of \(v\) (so its gradient, the acceleration, is momentarily zero).

parts.stem: (e) Find the exact displacement of the particle when \(t=\pi\), given that its initial displacement is 3 metres to the right of the origin.
parts.hint: Integrate \(v\) to find \(x\) (with a constant \(C\)), use \(x(0)=3\) to find \(C\), then substitute \(t=\pi\).

steps.explain: Integrate the velocity function to find displacement, including the constant of integration.
Use the initial condition \(x(0)=3\) to find \(C\).
Substitute \(t=\pi\) into the full displacement equation.
Simplify.
steps.work: \(x = 2\pi+3\) metres to the right of the origin.

questions.stem: A particle moves in a straight line. At time \( t \) seconds, its distance \( x \) metres from a fixed point \( O \) is given by \( x=1-\cos2t \), for \( 0\le t\le\pi \).

parts.stem: (a) Sketch the graph of \( x \) as a function of \( t \) for \( 0\le t\le\pi \).
parts.answer: A cosine-shaped curve: starts at \( (0,0) \), rises to a maximum \( (\tfrac{\pi}{2},2) \), then falls back to \( (\pi,0) \).

steps.explain: Step 1: Identify the key features of the trigonometric function \( x = 1 - \cos(2t) \). The principal axis (centre line) is at \( x=1 \). The amplitude is 1. The period is \( \dfrac{2\pi}{2} = \pi \).
Step 2: Find the key coordinates (start, quarter, half, three-quarters, and end of the period) by substituting \( t = 0, \dfrac{\pi}{4}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{3\pi}{4}, \pi \).
steps.work: t=0 \implies x=0 \\ t=\dfrac{\pi}{4} \implies x=1 \\ t=\dfrac{\pi}{2} \implies x=2 \\ t=\dfrac{3\pi}{4} \implies x=1 \\ t=\pi \implies x=0

steps.explain: Step 3: Plot these key points on a Cartesian plane and draw a smooth, continuous wave (an inverted cosine shape) passing through them.

parts.stem: (b) At what times is the particle at rest, and what is its position at those times?

steps.explain: The particle is at rest when its velocity is zero. Differentiate \( x \) with respect to \( t \) to find the velocity.
Set the velocity to zero and solve for \( t \) in \( 0\le t\le\pi \) (so \( 2t\in[0,2\pi] \)).
Substitute each value of \( t \) back into \( x=1-\cos2t \) to find the corresponding position.

parts.stem: (c) Find the velocity of the particle when \( t=\dfrac{\pi}{4} \).

steps.explain: Using the velocity function \( v=2\sin2t \) found in part (a), substitute \( t=\dfrac{\pi}{4} \).
Evaluate \( \sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}=1 \).

parts.stem: (d) For what values of \( t\in[0,\pi] \) is the particle’s velocity greater than 1 m/s?

steps.explain: Set up the inequality using \( v=2\sin2t \).
For \( t\in[0,\pi] \), \( 2t\in[0,2\pi] \) — one full cycle. \( \sin\theta>\tfrac12 \) holds for \( \theta \) strictly between \( \dfrac{\pi}{6} \) and \( \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \) in this range.
Divide every part of the inequality by 2 to solve for \( t \).

Part (a): sketch \(x=1-\cos2t\) for \(0 \le t \le \pi\). This is a cosine curve reflected and shifted: minimum \(x=0\) at \(t=0,\pi\) (where \(\cos2t=1\)), maximum \(x=2\) at \(t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) (where \(\cos2t=-1\)).

steps.explain: Part (b): find velocity by differentiating x with respect to t, then find when the particle is at rest (\(v=0\)).
Find the position at each of these rest times by substituting back into \(x=1-\cos2t\).
steps.work: At \(t=0\): \(x=1-\cos0=1-1=0\)\\ At \(t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\): \(x=1-\cos\pi=1-(-1)=2\)\\ At \(t=\pi\): \(x=1-\cos2\pi=1-1=0\)\\ So the particle is at rest at \(x=0\) (t=0 and t=π) and at \(x=2\) (\(t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\)).

steps.explain: Part (c): find the velocity at \(t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\) by substituting into \(v=2\sin2t\).
Part (d): solve the inequality \(v>1\) to find the time interval where velocity exceeds 1 m/s.

questions.stem: A particle moves with velocity \( v=\dfrac{4}{t+1}-2t \) for \( t\ge0 \).

parts.stem: (a) At what time does the particle change direction?

steps.explain: The particle changes direction when its velocity is momentarily zero.
Multiply through by \( (t+1) \) to clear the fraction, then rearrange into a quadratic.
Factorise and reject any solution outside the domain \( t\ge0 \). Pitfall: keeping the invalid negative root \( t=-2 \) as part of the answer.

parts.stem: (b) Find the exact distance travelled by the particle in the first 2 seconds.

steps.explain: Find the antiderivative (displacement function) of the velocity.
Since the particle changes direction at \( t=1 \), compute the displacement over \( [0,1] \) and \( [1,2] \) separately.

Distance is the sum of the absolute values of each displacement (since the particle reverses direction at t=1, one interval's displacement is negative). Pitfall: adding the signed displacements directly (instead of absolute values) understates the true distance travelled.

questions.stem: A particle moves in a straight line. At time \(t\) seconds, its distance \(x\) metres from a fixed point \(O\) on the line is given by \(x = 1-\cos 2t\).

parts.stem: (a) Sketch the graph of \(x\) as a function of \(t\) for \(0 \le t \le \pi\).

steps.explain: This is a cosine curve, reflected (due to the \(-\cos\)) and shifted up by 1. The amplitude is 1, midline is \(x=1\), and since the angle is \(2t\), the period is \(\dfrac{2\pi}{2}=\pi\).
Plot the key points: \(x(0)=1-\cos0=0\); \(x(\pi/2)=1-\cos\pi=2\) (maximum); \(x(\pi)=1-\cos2\pi=0\).
Sketch the smooth curve through these points, as shown above.
steps.work: Curve rises from \((0,0)\) to peak \((\pi/2,2)\), then falls back to \((\pi,0)\).

parts.stem: (b) Using your graph, or otherwise, find the times when the particle is at rest and the position of the particle at each of these times. Which of the following is correct?

steps.explain: The particle is at rest when its velocity \(v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0\) — on the graph, this is where the curve has a turning point (horizontal tangent).
Within \(0\le t\le\pi\), solve for \(t\) — these match the turning points visible on the graph in part (a): the start, the peak, and the end.
Read the corresponding \(x\)-position at each of these times directly from the graph (or the original equation).

parts.stem: (c) Find the velocity of the particle when \(t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\).

steps.explain: Differentiate \(x=1-\cos2t\) to find the velocity function.
Substitute \(t=\pi/4\).
Evaluate.

parts.stem: (d) When is the particle's velocity greater than \(1\text{ m/s}\) (for \(0 \le t \le \pi\))?
parts.hint: Solve \(2\sin 2t = 1\) first to find the critical values, then use the graph of \(v\) to see between which two times \(v>1\).

steps.explain: Find where \(v=1\) exactly, since these are the boundary (critical) values of the inequality.
Solve for \(2t\), then \(t\), within the extended range \(0 \le 2t \le 2\pi\).

Since \(v=2\sin2t\) rises from 0, peaks, then falls, it exceeds 1 only *between* these two critical times (not outside them) — this can be confirmed by testing a value like \(t=\pi/4\) from part (c), where \(v=2>1\), and \(\pi/4\) lies between \(\pi/12\) and \(5\pi/12\).
State the solution interval.

questions.stem: A particle moves along the \(x\)-axis. At a certain time, \(\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}=-2\text{ ms}^{-2}\) and \(\dfrac{dx}{dt}=1\text{ ms}^{-1}\). Which statement describes the motion of the particle at that time?
options: The particle is moving to the right with increasing speed.
The particle is moving to the left with decreasing speed.
The particle is moving to the right with decreasing speed.
The particle is moving to the left with increasing speed.
questions.hint: The sign of velocity gives the direction; when velocity and acceleration have opposite signs, the particle is slowing down (decelerating).

steps.explain: Velocity \(\dfrac{dx}{dt}=1>0\), so the particle is moving in the positive direction — to the right.
Acceleration \(\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}=-2<0\) is in the opposite direction to the velocity. When acceleration opposes velocity, the particle is decelerating (its speed is decreasing).
steps.work: Acceleration and velocity have opposite signs \(\;\Rightarrow\;\) speed decreasing

steps.explain: Combine both facts.
steps.work: \(\therefore\) moving to the right with decreasing speed

questions.stem: A particle moves along the \(x\)-axis, and after \(t\) seconds its displacement, \(x\) metres, is given by \(x = (t^2-1)^2\) metres. Find the acceleration of the particle, \(\ddot{x}\), as a function of \(t\).

steps.explain: Velocity is the first derivative of displacement. Use the chain rule on \(x=(t^2-1)^2\).
Acceleration is the derivative of velocity — differentiate \(\dot{x}\) with respect to \(t\).

questions.stem: The particle (with \(x=(t^2-1)^2, \ \dot{x}=4t^3-4t\)) initially moves left, before turning around and moving to the right. Find the particle's acceleration when it returns to its initial position.

steps.explain: The particle's INITIAL position is at \(t=0\). Find this value.
Find the next time \(t>0\) at which the particle returns to \(x=1\), by solving \(x(t)=1\).
Discard \(t^2=0\) (that's the starting time itself). Since \(t\) represents time, take the positive root of \(t^2=2\).
Substitute \(t=\sqrt{2}\) into the acceleration formula from part (a).
Calculate.

questions.stem: A particle \(P_1\) has acceleration \(\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2} = e^{-t}+e^{-2t}\) (in m/s\(^2\)). Initially, \(P_1\) is \(\dfrac34\) m to the right of the origin, travelling at velocity \(\dfrac{dx}{dt}=-\dfrac32\) m/s.

parts.stem: (a) Show that the displacement of the particle is given by \(x = e^{-t}+\dfrac14 e^{-2t}-\dfrac12\).

steps.explain: Integrate the acceleration once to find velocity, including a constant \(C_1\).
Use the initial condition \(\dot x(0) = -\tfrac32\) to solve for \(C_1\).
Integrate velocity once more to find displacement, including a constant \(C_2\).
Use the initial condition \(x(0)=\tfrac34\) to solve for \(C_2\).
Write the final displacement equation.

parts.stem: (b) Find the limiting displacement of \(P_1\), and hence state the limiting distance that \(P_1\) travels.
options: Limiting displacement \(=\dfrac34\) m; limiting distance travelled \(=\dfrac34\) m
Limiting displacement \(=-\dfrac12\) m; limiting distance travelled \(=\dfrac14\) m
Limiting displacement \(=-\dfrac12\) m; limiting distance travelled \(=1\dfrac14\) m
Limiting displacement \(=0\) m; limiting distance travelled \(=\dfrac12\) m
parts.hint: As \(t\to\infty\), both \(e^{-t}\) and \(e^{-2t}\) approach 0. The particle starts at \(\tfrac34\) and moves to this limiting position — the distance travelled is the size of that gap.

steps.explain: As \(t\to\infty\), both exponential terms decay to 0.
Substitute these limits into the displacement equation from part (a).

The particle starts at \(x=\tfrac34\) m (to the right of the origin) and moves steadily to \(x=-\tfrac12\) m (to the left of the origin) as \(t\to\infty\) — since it never reverses direction (velocity stays negative throughout, as \(-e^{-t}-\tfrac12e^{-2t}<0\) always), the total distance travelled is simply the size of this displacement change.

parts.stem: (c) A second particle \(P_2\) moves simultaneously, with acceleration \(\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2} = -e^{-t}-e^{-2t}\). It is also \(\dfrac34\) m to the right of the origin, travelling at velocity \(\dfrac{dx}{dt}=-\dfrac32\) m/s, when \(t=\ln3\) seconds. Determine the exact time when \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) are travelling at the same velocity. Do NOT simplify your answer.

steps.explain: Integrate \(P_2\)'s acceleration to get its velocity, including a constant \(c_3\).
Use the given condition for \(P_2\) — velocity \(=-\tfrac32\) at \(t=\ln3\) — to solve for \(c_3\), simplifying the exponentials using \(e^{-\ln3}=3^{-1}\) and \(e^{-2\ln3}=3^{-2}\).
Write P₁'s velocity (from part a's working) and \(P_2\)'s velocity, then set them equal to find when the two particles share the same velocity.
Set the two velocities equal and collect all terms on one side.
This is quadratic in \(e^{-t}\). Multiply through by 9 to clear the fraction, then apply the quadratic formula with \(u=e^{-t}\).
Since \(e^{-t}>0\) for all real \(t\), only the \(+\) root gives a valid solution.
Take the natural logarithm of both sides and solve for \(t\) (leaving the answer unsimplified, as instructed).

questions.stem: The velocity of a particle moving along the \(x\)-axis at \(v\) metres per second at \(t\) seconds is shown in the graph below (a straight line from \((0,3)\) to \((5,0)\)). Initially, the displacement \(x\) is equal to 13 metres.

parts.stem: (a) Write an equation that describes the displacement, \(x\), at time \(t\) seconds (for \(0\le t\le 5\)).
parts.hint: First find the equation of the line for \(v\) (gradient-intercept form), then integrate it to get \(x\), using \(x(0)=13\) to find the constant.

steps.explain: Find the equation of the velocity line: it passes through \((0,3)\) and \((5,0)\), giving gradient \(-\tfrac35\) and \(y\)-intercept 3.
Integrate \(v\) with respect to \(t\) to find displacement, including a constant \(C\).
Use the initial condition \(x(0)=13\) to solve for \(C\).
Write the final displacement equation.

parts.stem: (b) Draw a graph that shows the displacement of the particle, \(x\) metres from the origin, at time \(t\) seconds between \(t=0\) and \(t=6\). Label the coordinates of the endpoints of your graph.

steps.explain: For \(0\le t\le5\), use the displacement equation from part (a): a downward parabola. Its turning point (vertex) is at \(t=-\dfrac{b}{2a} = -\dfrac{3}{2(-3/10)} = 5\).

For \(t>5\), the particle moves at the constant velocity \(v=0\) reached at \(t=5\) — wait, checking the graph, \(v=0\) exactly at \(t=5\) (the line meets the \(t\)-axis there); beyond \(t=5\) the original velocity graph is not defined, but if the particle continues at the velocity it had approaching \(t=5\) extended as \(v=-\tfrac35t+3\) becomes negative, giving \(x(6) = -\dfrac{3}{10}(36)+18+13 = -10.8+31 = 20.2\).
Plot the endpoints \((0,13)\) and \((6,20.2)\), with the peak at \((5,20.5)\) in between, as shown on the graph above.

questions.stem: The population of an ant colony is modelled by \( P=1000e^{kt} \), where \( t \) is measured in weeks.

parts.stem: (a) Find the initial population (at \( t=0 \)).

steps.explain: The initial population occurs at \( t=0 \). Substitute this into the model.
Any number to the power 0 equals 1.

parts.stem: (b) After 5 weeks the population is 15 000. Find the exact expression and the value of \( k \), correct to 4 decimal places.

steps.explain: Substitute \( t=5 \) and \( P=15\,000 \) into the model \( P=1000e^{kt} \).
Divide both sides by 1000 to isolate the exponential term.
Take the natural logarithm of both sides to bring \( k \) out of the exponent.
Divide both sides by 5, then evaluate \( \ln15\approx2.7081 \).

parts.stem: (c) Using \( k=0.5416 \) from part (b), during which week will the population first exceed 50 000?

steps.explain: Set up the inequality for the population exceeding 50 000, using \( k=0.5416 \).
Divide both sides by 1000.
Take the natural logarithm of both sides to bring \( t \) out of the exponent.
Divide both sides by 0.5416, then evaluate.
Since \( t\approx7.22 \) weeks is between week 7 and week 8, the population first exceeds 50 000 during the 8th week.
Part (a): the initial population is found by substituting \(t=0\) into the model \(P=1000e^{kt}\).
Part (b): use the condition that at \(t=5\) weeks, the population is 15000, and substitute into the model.
Take the natural logarithm of both sides to solve for \(k\).
Evaluate to 4 decimal places, confirming the given value.
Part (c): find when the population first exceeds 50000 by substituting \(P=50000\) into the model and solving for t.
steps.work: \(50000 = 1000e^{0.5416t}\)\\ \(50 = e^{0.5416t}\)\\ \(\ln(50) = 0.5416t\)\\ \(t = \dfrac{\ln(50)}{0.5416} \approx \dfrac{3.912}{0.5416} \approx 7.22\text{ weeks}\)\\ Since \(t \approx 7.22\) falls after the end of week 7 (i.e. during the 8th week of growth), the population first exceeds 50000 during week 8.

questions.stem: A nest of insects has a population, \(P\), that grows exponentially so that \(\dfrac{dP}{dt} = 1200e^{0.3t}\), where \(t\) is in months. A nest had a population of 5000 after one month. A viable nest needs a population between 100 000 and 500 000. Determine how long it will take the nest to reach the viable stage (population = 100 000), correct to the nearest month.

steps.explain: Integrate the growth rate to find the population function.
Substitute the known condition \(P=5000\) at \(t=1\) to solve for \(C\).
Round \(C\) to the nearest whole number and write the full population equation.
Substitute \(P=100\,000\) and solve for \(t\), isolating the exponential term first.
Take the natural logarithm of both sides to solve for \(t\).
Evaluate and round to the nearest whole month.

questions.stem: The population of a white-ant colony is modelled by \(P=Ae^{kt}\), where \(A\) and \(k\) are positive constants and \(t\) is time in weeks. Initially, the population is 1000. Two weeks later, the population is 1500.

parts.stem: (a) Find the values of \(A\) and \(k\), expressed in exact form.
parts.hint: Use \(t=0, P=1000\) to find \(A\), then \(t=2, P=1500\) to find \(k\).

steps.explain: Substitute \(t=0, P=1000\) into the model.
Substitute \(t=2, P=1500\), using the value of \(A\) just found.
Take the natural log of both sides and solve for \(k\).

parts.stem: (b) Find the population after four weeks, correct to the nearest possible number of white-ants.
parts.hint: Substitute \(t=4\) into the model using the exact values of \(A\) and \(k\) from part (a).

steps.explain: Substitute \(t=4\) into the population model.
Evaluate and round to the nearest whole ant.

parts.stem: (c) White-ants can cause structural timber damage. This colony was found near a timber-framed home. Using the model, explain why the situation is getting worse over time. Show all mathematical working.

steps.explain: Differentiate the population model to find the rate of change of the population, \(\dfrac{dP}{dt}\).
Since \(k>0\), \(A>0\) and \(e^{kt}>0\) for all \(t\), the rate of change \(\dfrac{dP}{dt}\) is always positive — and it itself grows larger as \(t\) increases (since \(e^{kt}\) is increasing).
steps.work: \(\dfrac{dP}{dt} > 0\) for all \(t \ge 0\), and \(\dfrac{dP}{dt}\) is itself increasing over time

steps.explain: This means the population is not just increasing, but increasing at an ever-faster rate — exponential growth. Near a timber-framed home, this means the ant colony (and the structural damage risk) grows more rapidly the longer it is left unchecked.
steps.work: \(\therefore\) the population grows exponentially and increasingly rapidly, so the structural damage risk worsens more quickly over time.
